title: FunctionPointer and SharedStatic
sub: How to get a “virtual call” and shared statics in Burst, and what they cost
cards/0/title: Burst has no delegates and no virtual calls
cards/0/body:
A common question: “How do you do polymorphism in Burst?” First, why the usual route is closed. A virtual call needs a class object, and a delegate is a managed object too. Burst works only with unmanaged data: structs, pointers, native containers.

There are three substitutes, from simple to flexible:

  • a data tag and a switch — few variants, all known;
  • a generic job with an interface constraint — the variant is known at compile time;
  • FunctionPointer<T> — the variant is chosen at runtime, say from a level config.

A senior answer names all three and says what each one costs.
cards/1/body:
You need four things:

  • a delegate as the “interface” — a plain one, not generic: function pointers do not support generic delegates;
  • [BurstCompile] on the static method and on the type that holds it — otherwise Burst will not find the method;
  • [MonoPInvokeCallback(typeof(Delegate))] from the AOT namespace — for IL2CPP;
  • BurstCompiler.CompileFunctionPointer<T>(Method) — call it once from managed code and keep the result, a FunctionPointer<T>.

Parameters follow the native interop rules: numbers, pointers, ref to them. Structs, float4 included, go only by ref/in/out or by pointer, never by value; return a struct result through out. bool and char are not on the list of allowed types. NativeArray and most native containers cannot be passed: they carry managed safety-system fields.
cards/2/title: A FunctionPointer in a job is your “virtual call”
cards/2/body:
FunctionPointer<T> is a struct that holds the address of a compiled function. You can put it in a job field and call it with .Invoke(...). The main thread decides which function to call when it schedules the job: one job, different rules, and nothing to recompile.

For jobs, Burst compiles function pointers asynchronously, just like the jobs themselves.
cards/2/flow/1: Update: pick a pointer, put it in a job field
cards/3/q: Which delegates can be compiled into a FunctionPointer<T>? Select all that apply.
cards/3/explain: Numbers by value are fine. float4 is a struct, so only by in/out/ref: the second option is right, the third (float4 by value, and as the return) is not. A NativeArray cannot be passed because of its managed safety fields. Function pointers do not support generic delegates.
cards/4/title: The cost: an indirect call per element
cards/4/body:
A call through a pointer jumps to an address the compiler does not know. That costs three things:

  • no inlining — the function body is not merged into the loop;
  • no vectorization across the call — the function gets one scalar at a time, so there is no SIMD over four to eight elements at once;
  • no aliasing information — in a job Burst knows the containers do not overlap ([NoAlias] by default), a function pointer gets none of that.

The Burst docs say it plainly: use a job where you can. If you need a pointer, call it per batch, not per element: pass a pointer to the data and a count, and let the loop live inside the function. In the docs’ example, batches were 1.53× faster than per-element calls, and a plain IJobParallelFor without a pointer was another 1.26× faster than the batches.
cards/5/q: A job over a million elements calls rule.Invoke(...) for every element and is nearly twice as slow as the same job with the formula written right in Execute. What is the main reason?
cards/5/options/0: Every call is indirect: the function cannot be inlined, the loop cannot be vectorized, and there is no aliasing information
cards/5/options/1: Invoke allocates on the heap every time
cards/5/options/2: A FunctionPointer always runs on the main thread
cards/5/options/3: Burst copies the NativeArray on every call
cards/5/explain: A pointer is a jump to an unknown address. The compiler cannot see the function body, so it can neither inline it nor turn the loop into SIMD. The fix is batching (a pointer to the data plus a count) or a generic job if the rule is known at compile time.
cards/5/wrong/1: A FunctionPointer is a struct with an address; calling it allocates nothing.
cards/5/wrong/2: The pointer is called wherever the job runs — on a worker thread.
cards/5/wrong/3: You cannot pass an array to a function pointer at all; there is no copy, only the cost of the call itself.
cards/6/body:
If the variant is known at compile time, make the rule a struct that implements an interface, and make the job generic: struct MoveJob<TRule> : IJobParallelFor where TRule : struct, ISpeedRule. Burst compiles a separate version for each concrete type: the call rule.Speed(...) is known up front, so it can be inlined and vectorized together with the loop. Burst supports interface calls through a generic struct constraint.

The condition: a concrete type where you schedule — new MoveJob<Flee>. If the type arrives through a generic parameter, for instance the job is scheduled from a generic method Schedule<T>(), Burst will not find that version in a build: fast in the Editor, slow in the player. Burst does not support scheduling generic jobs through generic methods.

Summary: switch when there are few variants; generic when the type is known at compile time; FunctionPointer when the rule is chosen at runtime — and then in batches.
cards/7/task: Build a behaviour rule with a FunctionPointer. In the Rules class, write a static method Flee(float distance, float baseSpeed) that returns baseSpeed * 2, with the attributes [BurstCompile] and [MonoPInvokeCallback(typeof(SpeedRule))]. In MoveJob, add a FunctionPointer<Rules.SpeedRule> field and call it in Execute with Invoke(distance[i], baseSpeed). In RuleSetup.Compile, compile Rules.Flee with BurstCompiler.CompileFunctionPointer.
cards/7/checks/2/label: Flee matches the delegate signature and returns baseSpeed * 2
cards/7/checks/4/label: Execute calls the rule with .Invoke(distance[i], baseSpeed)
cards/7/explain: The attribute on the type and on the method lets Burst find the method; MonoPInvokeCallback is for IL2CPP. Compile once from managed code and cache it; the job gets a ready pointer. In the interview, add the cost: the call is indirect, so in a hot loop prefer batches or a generic job.
cards/8/body:
Burst can read static readonly fields: it evaluates them and the static constructors at compile time and bakes the values into the code. Burst code cannot write to an ordinary static field, and in a plain C# job statics have no protection at all and can crash the application.

If both C# and Burst code need mutable data, there is SharedStatic<T>: a piece of native memory both sides can see.

  • get it with SharedStatic<T>.GetOrCreate<Context, Key>() — a context type and an empty key class name the field;
  • .Data returns a ref T: read it, write it, take a ref;
  • initialise it from a static constructor in C# before Burst touches it, or the state is undefined.

The cost: it is global state. The safety system does not see it, so it will not catch a race from a parallel job. Write from many threads only atomically, with Interlocked (allowed in Burst). Use it for global flags, settings and debug counters, and pass a job its data through fields and containers.
cards/9/q: This job is scheduled with Schedule(n, 64), and the counter ends up lower than it should be. Which line is to blame?
cards/9/explain: Data++ means read, add, write. Two worker threads read the same value, and one of the increments is lost. The safety system cannot see this race: a SharedStatic is not a native container. Use Interlocked.Increment(ref Stats.Hits.Data) or, better, count per thread and add up after the job.
cards/10/q: Match the task to the tool.
cards/10/pairs/0/0: The rule comes from the level config at runtime
cards/10/pairs/1/0: Three behaviours, known at compile time, a hot loop
cards/10/pairs/1/1: a generic job with where T : struct, an interface
cards/10/pairs/2/0: A counter that both C# and Burst code read and write
cards/10/pairs/3/0: A table of constants that never changes
cards/11/q: Interviewer: “How do you make a virtual call in Burst?” Which answer is stronger?
cards/11/options/0: Burst has no delegates or virtual calls — those are managed objects. If the variant is known at compile time, I use a generic job with a struct rule: Burst instantiates it and the call can be inlined. If it is chosen at runtime, I use a FunctionPointer<T> from CompileFunctionPointer, but the call is indirect, with no inlining or vectorization, so I call it on a batch of data
cards/11/options/1: I put objects implementing an interface into a NativeArray and call the interface method in Execute
cards/11/options/2: I use a FunctionPointer<T>: Burst inlines it, so it costs the same as a normal call
cards/11/options/3: You can’t; Burst only has a switch over an enum
cards/11/explain: A strong answer names the mechanism (why it is not allowed), the two working routes and their cost. That is what marks a senior: not “there is FunctionPointer”, but when you need it and how not to lose speed on it.
cards/11/wrong/1: You cannot put a class object into a NativeArray: the container holds only unmanaged structs.
cards/11/wrong/2: A call through a pointer is indirect: the compiler does not know the address and cannot inline the function.
cards/11/wrong/3: A switch is only the simplest route; a generic job and FunctionPointer work too.
